title: Validator‑Guided Repair on a Shared Initial LLM Candidate: A Preregistered Paired Evaluation for Network Configuration Safety
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory study (PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01) that measured the downstream effect of a deterministic validator plus an allowed single automated repair on the exact same sampled LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics). Using the declared generator gpt‑5‑mini (hosted adapter) and a deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) on N=200 paired intents (completed_episode_count = 400; model_calls_used = 200), every shared initial candidate passed validator checks so no repairs were attempted or applied (repair_attempt_count = 0; repair_applied_count = 0). Observed outcomes: baseline_success = 200/200, guarded_success = 200/200; paired contingency n11=200, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0; exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) = [0.0, 0.0]. We provide artifact‑grounded methodological detail, representative validator diagnostics, reproducibility mappings, and a focused discussion clarifying the causal limits of the executed estimand under shared_initial_candidate semantics and concrete preregistered follow‑on designs to evaluate repair efficacy under independent sampling or adversarial conditions.

sections.introduction:
Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed for intent→configuration workflows in network operations (NetOps). However, LLM outputs may contain syntactic errors, logically inconsistent sequences, or hallucinated fields that, if executed, could violate redundancy or availability constraints. A common proposed mitigation is a generate–validate–repair (GVR) architecture: generate a candidate configuration, apply a deterministic validator to detect violations, and optionally trigger automated repair. Prior work shows verifier‑guided feedback can reduce incorrect artifacts in related domains (infrastructure‑as‑code, program repair), but transferability to NetOps device‑level execution remains an open empirical question [3,4].

This paper reports a fully preregistered, paired confirmatory experiment that implemented the shared_initial_candidate estimand: for each intent, exactly one sampled initial generation was produced and deterministically reused for both baseline (no validator/repair) and guarded (validator + ≤1 repair) arms. Under these semantics any paired difference can only arise from downstream validation/repair applied to that identical candidate; sampling variability across conditions is excluded by design. Our contributions are (1) a detailed, artifact‑grounded report of the executed paired experiment (N=200 pairs) including validator traces and execution accounting; (2) numeric inferential results for the executed estimand showing a degenerate null effect and explicit diagnostics explaining why repairs never executed; and (3) concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations and preregistered follow‑on estimands needed to measure repair efficacy under independent sampling, higher difficulty, or adversarial settings.
sections.related_work: Hallucination and unreliable references in LLM outputs are widely documented as trust problems for operational applications and motivate grounding and verification strategies [1]. Retrieval‑augmented and evidence‑grounded pipelines can reduce hallucination in operations‑style QA but typically evaluate textual correctness rather than device‑level executability in packet‑level simulators [2]. Verifier‑guided architectures (generate→verify→repair) have demonstrated empirical improvements for infrastructure‑as‑code and program generation (e.g., TerraFormer) by closing the loop with deterministic checks and feedback to the generator; these works motivate analogous NetOps pipelines but do not present standardized execution‑level device emulation results in the supplied corpus [3]. Recent NetOps LLM evaluations focus on intent translation and capability measurement; a consistent execution‑level safety benchmark in packet‑level simulation is not present among the verified records and therefore motivated our preregistered confirmatory test [4]. Our study is deliberately narrow: it tests the downstream effect of validator/repair on an identical sampled candidate rather than testing sampling, prompt engineering, or multi‑model generality.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment was preregistered as PREREG‑CAND‑001‑VER‑GVR‑2026‑09‑01 before any model calls. The primary estimand is the paired difference in the proportion of validator‑valid executable configurations between guarded and baseline conditions under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The design fixed task_count = 200 paired intents (planned_episode_count = 400) and allowed at most one automated repair per guarded episode; generation semantics were explicitly shared_initial_candidate so each pair reused the same sampled initial generation. Primary hypothesis H1 was preregistered: GVR (validator + ≤1 repair) reduces executable unsafe configurations relative to baseline on the same sampled candidate (paired McNemar test), with confirmatory alpha = 0.05 and power planning based on a target absolute reduction of 10 percentage points.

Task bank, contamination checks, and selection. A deterministic task generator produced a fixed manifest of 200 synthetic 'intent_configuration_repair_v1' tasks; each manifest entry contains initial_state, required_sequence, difficulty annotations (e.g., "safe_access_service_transfer", "rolling_access_vlan_migration"), and a generation_seed for deterministic replay. Prior to model calls the preregistered contamination checks (SHA256 exact‑match and high‑similarity n‑gram thresholds) were executed; no exact‑match exclusions were flagged and the confirmatory sample remained intact. Representative task manifest fields and difficulty annotations are archived under execution/task_manifest.jsonl.

Generation and model configuration. Execution adhered to shared_initial_candidate semantics: exactly one sampled initial generation per intent was produced and deterministically reused in both baseline and guarded episodes. The declared generator was gpt‑5‑mini via a hosted adapter (provider label openai_responses) and the archived model_configuration.json records declared_model_version = "gpt‑5‑mini" and temperature = null (unset). We explicitly state that temperature = null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0; nondeterministic sampling remains possible. The provider audit recorded hosted_model_call_event_count = 200 and a single stage labeled shared_initial_generation = 200, consistent with preregistered sampling semantics.

Validator and repair pipeline. Scoring used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 with scoring_rule = "full_intent_constraint_validation" producing binary executable/invalid labels and structured validator traces (validation_before/validation_after, normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes). For guarded episodes a single automated repair attempt was permitted (preregistered maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1). Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the baseline condition reused the same sampled candidate without repair; only the guarded arm could alter that same candidate via the permitted repair if validator_detections occurred. All per‑episode validator traces and repair metadata are archived in execution/scoring/*.json.

Analysis plan and statistical procedures. The preregistered primary test was the exact two‑sided McNemar test on the 2×2 paired contingency table, supplemented by a paired bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval for the paired difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000). Missingness policy used complete_pair_primary: exclude incomplete pairs. Sensitivity analyses (preregistered) included treating missing/failed episodes as failures (failure‑as‑zero) but no such episodes occurred. Multiplicity: single confirmatory test (no multiplicity correction); exploratory subgroup tests (not performed for primary claim) would employ Benjamini–Hochberg FDR control.

Reproducibility and archival mappings. Key artifacts required to reproduce the executed estimand and analysis are archived and referenced in the evidence bundle: execution/raw_results.jsonl (raw per‑episode records), execution/model_configuration.json (declared model and temperature = null), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (deterministic tasks and seeds), execution/scoring/ (per‑episode validator traces), analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, analysis/condition_summary.csv, analysis/missingness_summary.csv, and analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json. The master prompt immutable reference is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). The disclosure contains the required concise provenance and human/autonomy boundary statements.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The execution manifest reports planned_episode_count = 400, completed_episode_count = 400, failed_episode_count = 0, model_calls_used = 200 (one shared initial generation per pair), and completed_pair_count = 200. The analysis missingness summary records complete_pairs = 200 and zero failed or unscorable episodes.

Primary outcomes and inferential results. The per‑condition summaries are baseline_successes = 200/200 and guarded_successes = 200/200 (success_rate = 1.0 for each condition). The paired contingency table (guarded vs baseline) observed n11 = 200, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the paired difference (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples) = [0.0, 0.0]. These analytic artifacts are archived under analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/condition_summary.csv.

Repair activity, validator diagnostics, and representative examples. Across the confirmatory sample repair_attempt_count = 0 and repair_applied_count = 0 because no shared initial candidate triggered a validator violation. Representative per‑episode JSON artifacts (execution/scoring/task‑000004‑baseline.json and task‑000004‑guarded.json) show identical shared_initial_candidate text and identical validation_after.normalized_configuration values for both baseline and guarded. A concrete example (task‑000004 shared initial candidate excerpt) is: "interface edge2 admin down\ninterface edge2 vlan 40\ninterface edge2 admin up\ninterface edge1 admin down"; parsed_command_count = 4 and required_command_count = 4 for that example and validator.valid = true. Representative diagnostics for additional hard tasks (task‑000005, task‑000006) are archived and summarized in Table 2.

Contamination, reconciliation, and provider audit. Preexecution contamination checks flagged no exact‑match leaks; analysis/contamination_summary.csv is empty. Deterministic reconciliation confirms episode accounting consistency and reports cross_condition_cache_key_reuse_observed = false. The provider audit shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 200, cache_hit_count = 0, cache_miss_count = 200, and stage_counts indicating shared_initial_generation = 200, consistent with a single shared generation per pair. All deterministic consistency checks passed and are archived in analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json.

Statistical interpretation. The executed estimand examined only the downstream effect of validator/repair on an identical sampled candidate. Because all shared initial candidates were validator‑valid, the guarded pipeline had no opportunity to repair and thus could not change outcomes. The observed degenerate contingency table (zero discordant pairs) yields analytic quantities that correctly represent the executed estimand (McNemar p = 1.0; bootstrap CI = [0.0,0.0]) but provide no information about repair efficacy under independent per‑condition sampling or under task distributions that produce validator‑detectable faults.
sections.discussion:
Causal scope and implications. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the experiment isolates downstream validator/repair effects on fixed sampled candidates; it does not test whether constrained prompting, prompt templates, or repeated independent sampling would change first‑pass generator quality because no independent per‑condition generations were produced. The degenerate null result is therefore an artifact‑grounded finding: for the sampled tasks, model, and generator seedings used in this run, the single sampled candidate per intent complied with the deterministic validator and no repair was applicable.

Threats to validity (expanded). Internal validity: sampling semantics intentionally eliminate sampling variability; this is a design choice that constrains internal causal claims to validator/repair on the same candidate. Construct validity: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 enforces a preregistered mapping from intent constraints to validation checks (syntax, required sequence, dependency rules, protected interfaces). The validator is an abstraction: it does not execute vendor‑specific CLI or packet flows, so some real‑world failure modes (timing, protocol interactions) are not represented. External validity: a single declared model (gpt‑5‑mini via hosted adapter), a synthetic deterministic task bank, and a single validator implementation limit generalization beyond the studied setting. Conclusion validity: absence of discordant outcomes limits inference about repair efficacy under sampling variability; any affirmative claim about repair benefit under independent sampling would require a different preregistered estimand and dataset with higher expected validator‑detectable fault rate.

Operational recommendations grounded in artifacts. Using the archived pipeline and artifacts we recommend the following preregistered follow‑on experiments (each changes the estimand and is therefore a new confirmatory test): (A) independent per‑condition sampling: remove shared_initial_candidate semantics so baseline and guarded arms receive independent first‑pass generations (paired effect then conflates generation variability and repair and enables repair to act on a greater set of validator‑detected faults); (B) difficulty/adversary uplift: draw a targeted subset of tasks with "extreme" difficulty annotations from the task manifest or inject adversarial perturbations to increase expected validator failure rate; (C) explicit sampling control: set concrete numeric temperatures in model_configuration.json (rather than leaving temperature = null) and preregister parameter sweeps to examine tradeoffs between diversity and validator failure rate; (D) validator fidelity uplift: integrate vendor CLI semantics or packet‑level emulation to ensure repairs are evaluated against dynamic runtime behavior; (E) multi‑model, multi‑provider sampling to explore generality. Each follow‑on is supported by archived artifacts and clearly alters the estimand needed to assess repair efficacy in practice.

Why artifact grounding matters. The per‑episode JSONs (execution/scoring/) record validator.validation_before/after subtables, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, normalized_configuration, and repair_applied indicators; these artifacts make transparent why repairs never executed and allow independent reanalysis of the executed estimand without ambiguity about sampling semantics. The master prompt reference and model_configuration.json make explicit the declared generator and the temperature = null archival state; these provenance artifacts are necessary for reproducible confirmatory testing and for designing follow‑on preregistrations that change sampling parameters.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired confirmatory experiment designed to measure the downstream effect of deterministic validation and an allowed single automated repair on the exact same sampled LLM candidate per intent (shared_initial_candidate semantics). With gpt‑5‑mini as the declared generator and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the scorer, every shared candidate passed validation and no repairs were attempted or applied; guarded and baseline outcomes were identical for the executed estimand (paired difference = 0.0; McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap CI = [0.0, 0.0]). This result is narrowly scoped and artifact‑grounded: it demonstrates that under the sampled tasks and the shared_initial_candidate design there was no opportunity for repair to change outcomes, and it does not imply that GVR pipelines are unnecessary in general. As recommended above, follow‑on preregistered experiments that (1) remove shared_initial_candidate semantics, (2) increase task difficulty or introduce adversarial inputs, (3) set explicit sampling parameters, and (4) raise validator fidelity are required to empirically evaluate repair efficacy under realistic sampling variability and adversarial conditions. The archived artifacts and deterministic reconciliation support independent verification of the executed estimand and facilitate precise preregistered extensions. In short: the executed study validates the artifacted pipeline and clarifies an estimand boundary; measuring repair effectiveness under independent sampling remains an open, preregistered empirical task that our artifacts are prepared to support.

limitations: Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the design produced exactly one sampled initial generation per intent and reused it across baseline and guarded conditions; this measures validator/repair effects only and cannot detect differences caused by independent per‑condition sampling or prompt engineering.

Temperature unset (temperature = null) in the archived model configuration: null/unset is not evidence of deterministic sampling and does not imply temperature = 0; sampling nondeterminism may still have occurred during the single sampled generation.
Single model and single hosted provider: results reflect gpt‑5‑mini under the archived adapter; generalization to other models or model families is unsupported by these artifacts.

Synthetic task bank and validator abstraction: tasks were synthetic 'intent_configuration_repair_v1' items and the deterministic validator is an abstraction; realistic vendor CLI idiosyncrasies, emergent runtime interactions, and hardware effects were not executed on live devices.

No observed validator failures: all initial candidates were validator‑valid, so the experiment could not assess the repair step's effectiveness; the null effect therefore reflects the task bank and sampling semantics rather than evidence that GVR is unnecessary in general.
